# Introduction

India's five largest metropolitan areas — Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, and
Bengaluru span Indo-Gangetic Plain, the western and eastern coasts, the Deccan plateau, and the Bay of Bengal. Each city has a distinct pollution profile shaped by topography, industry, traffic, and climate.

This vignette uses the `vayuayanR` package to ask a single question across all
five cities:

> **How does PM2.5 pollution vary across India's major metros — seasonally,
> spatially, and in terms of monitoring coverage?**

We use two independent data sources throughout:

- **WUSTL ACAG V5GL04** — satellite-derived PM2.5 at ~1km resolution
- **CPCB CAAQMS** — ground-level monitoring station readings

---

# Data & Methods

## Satellite Data

Monthly PM2.5 estimates from WUSTL ACAG V5GL04 (~1km resolution, 1998–2022).
Files are read using a fast bounding-box subsetting approach that avoids loading
the full 121MB global array.

## Ground Data

City-level daily PM2.5 downloaded from the CPCB data repository using
`cpcb_download_city_data()`. Monthly means are computed from daily readings.

## Cities

| City      | Region        | CPCB Stations | Geography         |
|-----------|---------------|---------------|-------------------|
| Delhi     | North India   | 46            | Landlocked, IGP   |
| Mumbai    | West Coast    | 29            | Coastal peninsula |
| Kolkata   | East India    | 7             | River delta, IGP  |
| Chennai   | South Coast   | 9             | Coastal, Bay      |
| Bengaluru | Deccan Plateau| 14            | Inland, elevated  |

## Comparison Note

Ground readings are consistently higher than satellite estimates due to
point-source siting bias. All comparisons within this vignette use the same
methodology across cities, making relative comparisons valid even if absolute
values differ between sources.

## Helper Functions

```{r helper-functions}
read_v5gl04_fast <- function(nc_path, shape) {
  bbox    <- sf::st_bbox(shape)
  nc      <- ncdf4::nc_open(nc_path)
  lons    <- ncdf4::ncvar_get(nc, "lon")
  lats    <- ncdf4::ncvar_get(nc, "lat")
  lon_idx <- which(lons >= bbox["xmin"] & lons <= bbox["xmax"])
  lat_idx <- which(lats >= bbox["ymin"] & lats <= bbox["ymax"])
  data    <- ncdf4::ncvar_get(
    nc, "GWRPM25",
    start = c(min(lon_idx), min(lat_idx)),
    count = c(length(lon_idx), length(lat_idx))
  )
  ncdf4::nc_close(nc)
  mean(data, na.rm = TRUE)
}

load_v5gl04_rast <- function(year, month, shape) {
  nc_path <- sprintf(
    "/NAS/climatehealth/WUSTL_PM2.5/V5GL04/Global/Monthly/V5GL04.HybridPM25.Global.%04d%02d-%04d%02d.nc",
    year, month, year, month
  )
  bbox    <- sf::st_bbox(shape)
  nc      <- ncdf4::nc_open(nc_path)
  lons    <- ncdf4::ncvar_get(nc, "lon")
  lats    <- ncdf4::ncvar_get(nc, "lat")
  lon_idx <- which(lons >= bbox["xmin"] & lons <= bbox["xmax"])
  lat_idx <- which(lats >= bbox["ymin"] & lats <= bbox["ymax"])
  data    <- ncdf4::ncvar_get(
    nc, "GWRPM25",
    start = c(min(lon_idx), min(lat_idx)),
    count = c(length(lon_idx), length(lat_idx))
  )
  ncdf4::nc_close(nc)
  r <- terra::rast(
    nrows = length(lat_idx), ncols = length(lon_idx),
    xmin  = min(lons[lon_idx]), xmax = max(lons[lon_idx]),
    ymin  = min(lats[lat_idx]), ymax = max(lats[lat_idx]),
    crs   = "EPSG:4326"
  )
  terra::values(r) <- t(data)[nrow(t(data)):1, ]
  r
}
```

---

# Results

## The Season: How Does PM2.5 Vary Through the Year?

The first question is whether all five cities follow the same seasonal rhythm.
Geography and climate should produce very different patterns — but do the data
confirm this?

### Ground Data: City-Level Monthly Means

```{r ground-seasonal}
# Download city-level data for all five cities (cached after first run)
city_files <- list(
  Delhi     = "delhi_aqi_2022.csv",
  Mumbai    = "mumbai_aqi_2022.csv",
  Kolkata   = "kolkata_aqi_2022.csv",
  Chennai   = "chennai_aqi_2022.csv",
  Bengaluru = "bengaluru_aqi_2022.csv"
)

city_download_names <- list(
  Delhi     = "Delhi",
  Mumbai    = "Mumbai",
  Kolkata   = "Kolkata",
  Chennai   = "Chennai",
  Bengaluru = "Bengaluru"
)

for (city in city_names) {
  if (!file.exists(city_files[[city]])) {
    cpcb_download_city_data(
      city          = city_download_names[[city]],
      year          = 2022,
      save_location = city_files[[city]]
    )
  }
}

# Read and reshape — detect whether first column is Day or Date
ground_monthly <- map_dfr(city_names, function(city) {
  df      <- read.csv(city_files[[city]])
  day_col <- names(df)[1]
  df %>%
    pivot_longer(cols = -all_of(day_col),
                 names_to = "Month_Name", values_to = "pm25") %>%
    mutate(month = match(Month_Name, month.name)) %>%
    filter(!is.na(pm25), !is.na(month)) %>%
    group_by(month) %>%
    summarise(ground_pm25 = mean(pm25, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(city = city)
})

print(
  ground_monthly %>%
    pivot_wider(names_from = city, values_from = ground_pm25) %>%
    arrange(month)
)
```

### Satellite Data: Monthly Spatial Means

```{r satellite-seasonal}
# Load city boundaries
shape_files <- list(
  Delhi     = "/NAS/darakshann/geojson/delhi_gadm.geojson",
  Mumbai    = "/NAS/darakshann/geojson/mumbai_v4.geojson",
  Kolkata   = "/NAS/darakshann/geojson/kolkata.geojson",
  Chennai   = "/NAS/darakshann/geojson/chennai.geojson",
  Bengaluru = "/NAS/darakshann/geojson/bengaluru.geojson"
)

# Load all city shapes
city_shapes <- map(city_names, function(city) {
  sf::st_read(shape_files[[city]], quiet = TRUE) %>%
    sf::st_make_valid() %>%
    sf::st_union()
})
names(city_shapes) <- city_names

# Extract monthly satellite means for all cities
sat_monthly <- map_dfr(city_names, function(city) {
  shape <- city_shapes[[city]]
  map_dfr(1:12, function(m) {
    nc_file <- sprintf(
      "/NAS/climatehealth/WUSTL_PM2.5/V5GL04/Global/Monthly/V5GL04.HybridPM25.Global.2022%02d-2022%02d.nc",
      m, m
    )
    tibble(
      city    = city,
      month   = m,
      sat_pm25 = read_v5gl04_fast(nc_file, shape)
    )
  })
})
```

### Seasonal Line Chart — All Cities

```{r seasonal-chart, fig.height=7, fig.cap="Monthly mean PM2.5 across five Indian metros, 2022. Solid lines = CPCB ground data, dashed lines = WUSTL satellite estimates. WHO 24-hour guideline (15 µg/m³) shown as reference. Delhi operates in a fundamentally different pollution regime from all other cities."}

# Combine ground and satellite
seasonal_combined <- ground_monthly %>%
  left_join(sat_monthly, by = c("city", "month"))

# WHO reference
who_annual <- 5
who_24hr   <- 15

ggplot(seasonal_combined, aes(x = month, color = city)) +
  # Ground lines (solid)
  geom_line(aes(y = ground_pm25), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(aes(y = ground_pm25), size = 2) +
  # Satellite lines (dashed)
  geom_line(aes(y = sat_pm25), linewidth = 0.7, linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.7) +
  # WHO guidelines
  geom_hline(yintercept = who_24hr, linetype = "dotted",
             color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 11.5, y = who_24hr + 8,
           label = "WHO 24hr (15)", size = 3, color = "grey4", hjust = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12, labels = month.abb) +
  scale_color_manual(values = city_colors, name = NULL) +
  labs(
    title    = "India's Metros: PM2.5 Seasonal Cycle (2022)",
    subtitle = "Solid = CPCB ground | Dashed = WUSTL satellite | Dotted = WHO 24hr guideline",
    y        = expression(paste("PM2.5 (", mu, "g/m"^3, ")")),
    x        = NULL,
    caption  = "Source: WUSTL ACAG V5GL04 + CPCB CAAQMS"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    text               = element_text(family = "Arial"),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    legend.position    = "top",
    plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle      = element_text(size = 9.5, color = "grey40")
  )

ggsave("fig1_metro_seasonal_comparison.png", width = 10, height = 7, dpi = 300)
```

> **Key finding:** Delhi operates in a fundamentally different pollution regime.
> Its winter peak exceeds all other cities by 3–5x. Mumbai, Chennai, and
> Bengaluru show broadly similar levels. Kolkata occupies a middle position,
> reflecting its location on the Indo-Gangetic Plain where meteorology
> concentrates pollutants in winter. All coastal cities show a sharper monsoon
> dip due to rainfall washout.

## The Worst Month: Where Is Pollution Highest Within Each City?

November is the peak pollution month for most Indian cities. The spatial
distribution within each city tells a different story depending on
geography and urban structure.

```{r heatmaps, fig.height=10, fig.cap="November 2022 satellite PM2.5 across five metros. Same colour scale across all panels for honest cross-city comparison. Delhi's northern districts dominate the scale — all other cities appear comparatively low but still exceed WHO limits."}

# Load November rasters for all cities
nov_rasters <- map(city_names, function(city) {
  shape <- sf::st_read(shape_files[[city]], quiet = TRUE) %>%
    sf::st_make_valid()
  r     <- load_v5gl04_rast(2022, 11, shape)
  terra::mask(r, terra::vect(sf::st_union(shape)))
})
names(nov_rasters) <- city_names

# Get global min/max for shared scale
all_vals  <- unlist(lapply(nov_rasters, function(r) terra::values(r, na.rm = TRUE)))
scale_min <- floor(min(all_vals, na.rm = TRUE))
scale_max <- ceiling(max(all_vals, na.rm = TRUE))


```

```{r}
# Build individual plots
heatmap_plots <- map(city_names, function(city) {
  shape <- sf::st_read(shape_files[[city]], quiet = TRUE) %>%
    sf::st_make_valid()
  boundary <- suppressWarnings(sf::st_union(shape))

  ggplot() +
    geom_spatraster(data = nov_rasters[[city]]) +
    geom_sf(data = boundary, fill = NA,
            color = "grey20", linewidth = 0.4) +
    scale_fill_distiller(
      palette   = "YlOrRd",
      direction = 1,
      limits    = c(scale_min, scale_max),
      na.value  = NA,
      name      = expression(paste("PM"[2.5]))
    ) +
    labs(title = city) +
    xlab(NULL) + ylab(NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(
      text             = element_text(family = "Arial"),
      panel.grid       = element_blank(),
      legend.position  = "none",
      plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5, size = 11)
    )
})

# Shared legend from Delhi (highest range)
legend_plot <- heatmap_plots[[1]] +
  scale_fill_distiller(
    palette   = "YlOrRd",
    direction = 1,
    limits    = c(scale_min, scale_max),
    na.value  = NA,
    name      = expression(paste("PM"[2.5] ~ (mu * g/m^3)))
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(fill = guide_colorbar(
    barwidth = unit(15, "lines"), barheight = unit(0.6, "lines"),
    title.position = "top"
  ))
# Replace the legend section with this simpler approach
wrap_plots(heatmap_plots, ncol = 3, guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(
    title    = "November 2022 PM2.5 Across India's Five Metros",
    subtitle = "Same colour scale across all cities | Source: WUSTL ACAG V5GL04",
    theme    = theme(
      plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "grey40")
    )
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

ggsave("fig2_metro_heatmaps_nov2022.png", width = 15, height = 9, dpi = 300)
```


> **Key finding:** On a shared scale, Delhi's northern districts dominate.
> Within each city, spatial gradients are clear — industrial zones and
> traffic corridors show consistently elevated PM2.5 regardless of city.

## The Network: Are Cities Well Monitored?

More stations does not always mean better coverage — it depends on city size
and where stations are placed. This section compares station density and
distribution across cities.

```{r station-network}
# Get station counts and coordinates for all cities
station_data <- map_dfr(city_names, function(city) {
  stations <- cpcb_get_station_list(city_download_names[[city]])
  tibble(
    city          = city,
    n_stations    = nrow(stations)
  )
})

# Compute city areas in km²
city_areas <- map_dfr(city_names, function(city) {
  shape <- sf::st_read(shape_files[[city]], quiet = TRUE) %>%
    sf::st_make_valid() %>%
    sf::st_union() %>%
    sf::st_transform(3857)  # project for area in metres
  tibble(
    city     = city,
    area_km2 = as.numeric(sf::st_area(shape)) / 1e6
  )
})

# Annual mean satellite PM2.5 per city (mean of 12 monthly means)
annual_sat <- sat_monthly %>%
  group_by(city) %>%
  summarise(annual_sat_pm25 = mean(sat_pm25, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# Annual mean ground PM2.5
annual_ground <- ground_monthly %>%
  group_by(city) %>%
  summarise(annual_ground_pm25 = mean(ground_pm25, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# Winter mean (Oct, Nov, Dec, Jan)
winter_ground <- ground_monthly %>%
  filter(month %in% c(1, 10, 11, 12)) %>%
  group_by(city) %>%
  summarise(winter_ground_pm25 = mean(ground_pm25, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# WHO exceedance: days where daily PM2.5 > 15 µg/m³
who_exceedance <- map_dfr(city_names, function(city) {
  df      <- read.csv(city_files[[city]])
  day_col <- names(df)[1]
  df %>%
    pivot_longer(cols = -all_of(day_col),
                 names_to = "Month_Name", values_to = "pm25") %>%
    filter(!is.na(pm25)) %>%
    summarise(
      city             = city,
      who_exceed_days  = sum(pm25 > 15, na.rm = TRUE),
      total_days       = sum(!is.na(pm25))
    )
})

# Combine all metrics
city_summary <- station_data %>%
  left_join(city_areas,    by = "city") %>%
  left_join(annual_sat,    by = "city") %>%
  left_join(annual_ground, by = "city") %>%
  left_join(winter_ground, by = "city") %>%
  left_join(who_exceedance, by = "city") %>%
  mutate(
    stations_per_100km2  = round(n_stations / area_km2 * 100, 2),
    who_exceed_pct       = round(who_exceed_days / total_days * 100, 1)
  )

print(city_summary)
```

## City Rankings

```{r rankings-table, fig.height=5, fig.cap="City rankings across key PM2.5 metrics, 2022. Cities ordered by annual mean ground PM2.5."}

# Prepare ranked table for plotting
rankings <- city_summary %>%
  select(city, annual_ground_pm25, winter_ground_pm25,
         annual_sat_pm25, n_stations, stations_per_100km2, who_exceed_pct) %>%
  arrange(desc(annual_ground_pm25)) %>%
  mutate(
    rank              = row_number(),
    annual_ground_pm25 = round(annual_ground_pm25, 1),
    winter_ground_pm25 = round(winter_ground_pm25, 1),
    annual_sat_pm25    = round(annual_sat_pm25, 1),
    stations_per_100km2 = round(stations_per_100km2, 2)
  )

print(rankings)


```

```{r}
# Bar chart — annual mean PM2.5 ranked
ggplot(rankings, aes(x = reorder(city, annual_ground_pm25),
                     y = annual_ground_pm25, fill = city)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 15, linetype = "dotted",
             color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.3) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.6, y = 18,
           label = "WHO 24hr (15)", size = 3, color = "grey4", hjust = 0) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(annual_ground_pm25, " µg/m³")),
            hjust = -0.15, size = 3.5, color = "grey20") +
  coord_flip(clip = "off") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = city_colors, guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.2))) +
  labs(
    title    = "Annual Mean PM2.5 — Five Indian Metros (2022)",
    subtitle = "CPCB ground station data | Dashed = WHO 24hr guideline",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = expression(paste("Annual mean PM2.5 (", mu, "g/m"^3, ")")),
    caption  = "Source: CPCB CAAQMS | 2022"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    text             = element_text(family = "Arial"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(linetype = "dotted",
             color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.3),
    plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle    = element_text(size = 9.5, color = "grey40")
  )

ggsave("fig4_metro_annual_ranking.png", width = 10, height = 5, dpi = 300)

```

> **Key finding:** All five cities exceed the WHO 24-hour PM2.5 guideline on
> the majority of days. Delhi exceeds it by the widest margin — its annual mean
> is multiple times the WHO limit. Bengaluru and Chennai perform relatively
> better, but still exceed safe levels for most of the year.

---

# Discussion

## Geography Drives the Seasonal Story

The most striking finding from the seasonal analysis is how strongly geography
shapes pollution patterns. Delhi and Kolkata — both on the Indo-Gangetic Plain —
show the most pronounced winter peaks. The IGP acts as a natural trap: the
Himalayas block cold northern winds from dispersing pollutants, and shallow
temperature inversions concentrate emissions near the surface. Coastal cities
(Mumbai, Chennai) benefit from sea breezes that provide partial ventilation
year-round.

## Monsoon as the Great Equaliser

All five cities show a dip during the southwest monsoon (June–September), but
the magnitude differs dramatically. Delhi's monsoon PM2.5 is still above the
WHO annual limit. Chennai and Bengaluru approach near-safe levels in the
wettest months, reflecting both lower baseline emissions and more efficient
rainfall-driven washout.

## Monitoring Coverage

The station density analysis reveals that monitoring investment does not always
match pollution burden. Delhi, despite being the most polluted city, has the
highest absolute station count — but its vast geographic extent means coverage
per km² varies considerably. Smaller cities with fewer stations may have larger
unmonitored areas proportionally.

---

# Limitations

- **Satellite data version**: V5GL04 covers 1998–2022. The methodology is
identical for any year once V6GL02 is available.

- **City boundary files**: Results are sensitive to how city boundaries are
defined. Administrative boundaries may not correspond to the functional urban
area where pollution is generated and measured.

- **Station count only**: This analysis counts stations but does not assess
their spatial distribution within each city. A city could have many stations
clustered in one area and large unmonitored zones elsewhere.

- **2022 only**: A single year may not represent the long-term pollution
climatology of each city. Year-to-year variability, particularly in monsoon
intensity, can shift annual means significantly.

- **Ground data aggregation**: City-level CPCB data represents a mean across
all active stations. Cities with fewer stations (Kolkata: 7, Chennai: 9) may
have less representative city-level averages than Delhi (46 stations).
